a) Equal Opportunity in Employment: Each of the housing producers and site developers has been required to develop and implement equal opportunity programs in his recruiting, training, employment and promotion activities. Guidelines prepared by the Department were provided to each of the program participants to set the framework for these programs, and the resulting program plans and implementation have been closely monitored.
b) Equal Opportunity in Housing: Fair marketing guidelines establishing affirmative marketing programs have been developed for the program as a fore-runner for similar guidelines now established for all HUD-supported housing activities. These guidelines require that affirmative action be taken with regard to advertising, selection of sales agents, site processing and all other aspects of housing marketing.
iii. Impact on Department Policy Planning
In parallel to the experimental activities in the social elements of the program just noted, the Department commissioned the National Academy of Sciences - National Research Council to examine the question of "social mixing" in housing, and to see what information from the behavioral and social sciences could be applied to the theoretical aspects of this program. A Social Science Panel, attached to both the NAS-NRC Division of Behavioral Sciences and ACHUD, has commissioned various studies, reviewed the literature and other sources, and presented a report, "Freedom of Choice in Housing," to HUD as a basis for future policy planning.
3. POTENTIAL ADVERSE ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS
A number of adverse effects on the local environment could develop from the BREAKTHROUGH prototype sites. Each of these have been addressed in the program plan, and it is considered that any resultant effect will be far outweighed by the positive environmental aspects of the program.
A. Changes in Storm Runoff
Any developmental project which takes land from an unused or agricultural condition and constructs housing, other buildings and roadways will affect the storm runoff pattern. The foregoing discussion outlines the solutions being undertaken in BREAKTHROUGH to control this change.
B. Visual Effect of Change in Use
A housing development placed in an open area can become a visual nightmare. Careful attention to housing system placement, massing, and finishes has been directed to overcome this potential problem.
